title: Refining Hybrid Genetic Search for CVRP via RL-Finetuned LLM
one_liner: Train a small language model with reinforcement learning to automatically write better crossover operators for genetic algorithms that solve vehicle routing problems.
lead: Vehicle routing (deciding which trucks visit which customers) is a hard optimization problem that usually requires either expert human design or prompting massive models like GPT-4. This paper shows that a smaller language model (14 billion parameters) can be fine-tuned to automatically write better operators—the mixing rules that combine solutions in genetic algorithms—than human experts designed, because training it with step-by-step rewards teaches it to avoid the traps that trap un-trained models. The trick is a rewards system that teaches the model step by step: first to write valid code, then code that runs, then code that actually solves the problem better, because this progression mirrors how humans learn—mastering basics before tackling hard tasks.

problem.h2: The routing riddle: why hand-made rules break
paras: Imagine a delivery company with ten trucks and 100 stores to visit. The company must decide which truck visits which stores, respecting fuel limits and delivery time windows. This is called vehicle routing. For decades, solving it meant either hiring experts to hand-write specialized rules or—recently—asking a massive general-purpose model like GPT-4 to generate code.

The hand-written rules work well but require deep expertise and manually trying dozens of approaches. The big models (GPT-4) require sending your problem to the cloud every time and cost money, and they were not trained specifically for routing. A natural thought arises: would a smaller model, trained on routing data specifically instead of everything, match their performance because focused learning can concentrate capability?

callout.html: Yes—if you teach it step by step with rewards that start simple and gradually get harder, and prevent it from copying old solutions.

steps.text: Ask the small model: write me a crossover operator for vehicle routing.
Did the code have valid syntax (could a computer read it)? If yes, give reward +1.
Does the code actually execute without crashing? If yes, give a bigger reward.

Test the operator on known routing puzzles. Measure solution cost versus the expert operator, because that difference is the signal the learning algorithm uses to steer the model toward writing good code.
Use the rewards to nudge the language model: repeat patterns that earned high rewards, avoid those that earned low.

paras: The paper modifies the training rewards for the language model: instead of one simple goal (make the solution better), it uses a ladder of three goals. First: write code that is syntactically valid, because a language model without syntax training generates garbage symbols. Second: write code that actually runs, because syntax is not enough if the code crashes. Third: write code that makes solutions better than the expert baseline, because only this final stage teaches the algorithm to produce something useful. This ladder teaches the model gradually, the way a student learns algebra before calculus.

hidden.name: Solution quality gap: generated operator versus expert baseline
paras: The paper measures something it does not name in a headline: the quality of the crossover operators produced by the language model. This is measured by running each generated operator on a set of known routing problems and seeing how good the solutions are—specifically, how much improvement it gives over the hand-designed baseline operator, because without a baseline to compare to, we cannot tell if the model is learning or just guessing.

The metric is simple: take a routing problem the LLM has never seen, run the generated operator, measure the solution quality, and compare to what the expert operator achieves. The difference (better or worse) is the signal that trains the model, because the learning algorithm uses this comparison to nudge the model toward patterns that find better solutions.

heat.caption: Darker means operators find lower cost routes. Highlight shows which operators the training rewards toward.

reads.html: The model learns to write code that solves the routing problem better than a human expert wrote it, because the rewards system gives high scores to code that finds lower-cost routes.

The reward function assigns a scalar value (the improvement of the operator on a test set relative to the baseline) that the reinforcement learning algorithm uses to optimize the language model policy, adjusting the probability of generating similar patterns when the reward was high and avoiding them when the reward was low.

mechanism.h2: Why step-by-step rewards beat single-step rewards
paras: Language models were trained to predict the next word, not to write code. If you simply ask one to write a routing operator without teaching it step by step, it often produces words that look like code but have syntax errors or run-time crashes. Jumping straight to 'write code that solves the problem' fails because the model has not yet learned the basics.

The paper's curriculum fixes this with a three-level ladder. First, the model learns what valid code looks like (getting rewarded for syntax). Second, it learns that code must not crash (getting rewarded for execution). Third—only after it has mastered those—it learns to write code that produces good solutions. This is the same way a student learns: letters first, then words, then meaning. Each level makes the next level possible.

stages.s: Prompt: write a crossover operator for routing
Check execution: does it run without crashing?
Test on known problems: measure routing solution cost against the expert operator
Reward score computed from syntax, execution, and solution quality

math.words: Total reward equals a base reward if the code compiles and runs, plus a solution improvement bonus if the operator beats the baseline on test problems.
math.equation: R = R_syntax + R_execute + R_quality, where R_quality = improvement_percent * scaling_factor
symbols: Total reward signal for this generated operator
Bonus points if the generated text is valid code
Bonus points if the code runs without crashing
Bonus based on how much better the solutions are versus the expert operator
A number (e.g., 10) that makes the quality reward big enough to matter

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Operator A generates code with syntax error: R_syntax=0, total R=0. Model learns to avoid this pattern.
Operator B generates valid code but crashes: R_syntax=1, R_execute=0, total R=1. Progress, but the model keeps learning.
Operator C generates valid, executable code but solutions are 5% worse than expert: R_syntax=1, R_execute=1, R_quality=(-0.05)*10=-0.5, total R=1.5. Barely passes.
Operator D generates valid, executable code that is 15% better than expert: R_syntax=1, R_execute=1, R_quality=(0.15)*10=1.5, total R=3.5. Big reward! Model learns this pattern.

math.note: The ladder of rewards (syntax, then execution, then quality) ensures the model learns to walk before it runs.

items.html: After generating many operators, the LLM might start repeating code it has already written (plagiarizing itself). The paper fixes this with an operator cache: if code is too similar to something seen before, it gets penalized. Without this, the model learns nothing new.

If a single test case gives wildly different results each time, the model cannot learn a consistent pattern. The solution: test each operator on many routing problems (e.g., 100 standard benchmarks) and average the result. A stable signal is learnable; randomness is not.

If the syntax and execution rewards are too small, the model might ignore them and jump straight to maximizing solution quality, producing mostly broken code. The paper ensures each reward level has enough points to matter before moving to the next.

items.b: Done right: small models can rival giant models.
items.html: When the three rewards are properly balanced and the model has access to feedback from many test problems, a 14-billion-parameter model (a thousand times smaller than some commercial models) can learn to write operators that beat the 140-billion-parameter GPT-4.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small vehicle routing problem (e.g., 50 stops, 5 trucks). Implement the hand-designed expert operator (a simple crossover rule). Train the LLM using RFTHGS for 200 generations, giving it rewards at each step. At the end, generate a final operator from the trained model and test it on 10 new routing problems it has never seen. Measure the solution quality of both the expert and the trained-model operator.
demo.closing: The demo is successful if the trained LLM operator finds solutions that cost 5-15% less than the expert operator, proving that the curriculum-based reward teaching actually transfers to new problems.
